title: Simplify, simplify
hookLine: our life is frittered away by detail: simplify, simplify (Walden 2)

cards: How many small decisions has today asked for so far? Which shirt. Which reply.
Which of four reminders first. Each one tiny, none worth a second thought. And yet by evening, a day like that can seem used up, though it's hard to say on what.

Thoreau had a word for this, long before inboxes. In the second chapter of Walden, on where he lived and what he lived for, he calls it frittering. And he answers it with one word, said again and again.

teach.b: First, the diagnosis: "Our life is frittered away by detail." Frittered is an exact word. Not stolen.
Not wasted in one big mistake. Crumbled away in small pieces, the way a cookie disappears in crumbs.
Second, the cry: "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" Three times, with an exclamation mark.

An honest person, he says, hardly needs to count past their ten fingers, in extreme cases adding the ten toes, and lumping the rest. He's joking, and he means it: keep your affairs few enough to count on your hands.
Third, the instruction: simplify. The word turns from a quality into a verb.

Simplicity is something you admire; simplify is something you do. His examples are deliberately blunt: fewer meals, if one will do, fewer dishes, and the rest reduced in proportion. The point isn't the menu.

Simplifying happens in specific, ordinary places, not in general. Fourth, simple isn't empty. This is the chapter where Thoreau explains why he went to the woods at all, to live deliberately, as day ninety-one put it.
Clearing the clutter was never the goal. It made room for what he called the essential, so that something could finally get his full attention. So the question isn't just what can I drop.
It's what am I clearing space for.

how: Some readers of Walden take 'simplify, simplify' as a working practice, trimming one routine or possession at a time to make room for what they count as essential.

o: throwing out nearly everything you own at once
making every task as fast and efficient as you can
Thoreau's verb: cut the details that fritter life away

p: enough to count your affairs on

s: Thoreau says life is lost mainly in one big mistake
he says it is frittered away by detail: lost in small pieces.
in the same passage Thoreau jokes about counting on fingers and toes
an honest person hardly needs to count past ten fingers, or in extreme cases ten toes, and lump the rest.
for Thoreau, simplifying means emptying life of everything
he clears away detail to make room for what's essential.

games.q: your days are frittered away by detail. what does Thoreau suggest?
o: add a better system to track the details.
simplify: keep affairs few enough to count on your fingers.
give up and accept the clutter.
games.why: he cries 'simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!' and jokes that ten fingers, or in extreme cases ten toes, should be enough to count your affairs.

practice: Pick one ordinary routine, getting ready in the morning, making dinner, the first hour at work, and walk through it in your mind, step by step.

Notice the small steps that crumble the time: the extra checking, the choosing, the things done only out of habit. Now picture the same routine with one step gone, just one, and feel how it is to move through it lighter.

wordCard.voice: Simplify. Thoreau's answer in Walden to a life frittered away by detail: keep your affairs few enough to count on your fingers, and clear room for what's essential. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: simplify. Less, so the essential gets the room. Back tomorrow, same hill.
